accuracy.evidence: Checked against CCSS ELA RL.K.5 (recognise common types of texts such as storybooks and poems), RL.K.6 and RI.K.6 (name the author and illustrator and define each role) and RL.1.5 (differences between books that tell stories and books that give information). The lesson says poems often rhyme rather than always, and names fiction as made up on purpose, not lies.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented early-reader errors: judging text type from the cover picture (lizard-cover prediction, lion and shark items), pictures mean a story (clue hunt rejects the picture and page number), the author draws the pictures (illustrator prediction and tag feedback), one person cannot do both jobs (Ana Ruiz cover), and every poem rhymes (m8).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtexts is built around books themselves: a three-shelf library sort with cover traps, a page clue hunt where only the words count, a cover where pencil and paintbrush role tags are dropped on the author and illustrator lines, a rhyme-pair finder and a make-your-own book that labels its type from the words chosen. The 6-token shingle gate passed against every other flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Children find out by doing: the All About Lizards card bounces off the Story shelf with a reason, tapping a picture or page number on a page says every book has those, and the book they make is called a story, poem or fact book only from the words they picked, so they discover that the words decide the type.

predictions.evidence: Two locked predictions with a tempting wrong option: a lizard on the cover means a story (disproved when the lizard book only fits Facts) and the author draws the pictures (disproved by dropping the paintbrush tag on the pictures-by line, then by a cover where one person does both).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with ten tagged wrong answers (story, poem, illus, reader, fact, long, cover, pages, none, tell). Each message names the slip, for example that hop and stop rhyme so it is a poem, or that words and pictures by Jo Park means Jo is author and illustrator.

readability.evidence: Family audience: kid text FK 2.2 against the 5.0 target and adult text FK 5.9 against 10.0, from learn/readability.py. Kid sentences are short and concrete (story, poem, fact book, cover, author, illustrator); the adult notes use the exact terms fiction, non-fiction, title, contents page, label and caption.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean and explanation overlap with other lessons under 12 percent. Each kid paragraph adds one idea (three types, the cover can trick you, clues inside, author and illustrator); adult paragraphs give the standards, terms, named mistakes and what each lab step does.

mobile.evidence: iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light for all six steps: six book cards sit in two rows of three above three shelves, the cover and tags stack vertically, poem lines are full-width tap rows and the make-a-book cards fit three across. phone_sweep reported 0 findings and walk.cjs passed on iPhone 13 and desktop.

accessibility.evidence: axe finds no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme. Every drag has a tap-then-tap route and a button route (shelf buttons, tag-to-name buttons, poem line buttons, words and picture buttons), the young class enlarges controls, and the canvas aria-label and live region read every result aloud.
